ludwig-crocius.name: Ludwig Crocius
ludwig-crocius.bio: Bremen Reformed pastor and professor at the Gymnasium Illustre. A Dort delegate for Bremen, he stood for Melanchthonian irenicism and moderate orthodoxy rather than high Calvinist strictness, and his Syntagma sacrae theologiae (1636) is the chief systematic statement of that Bremen school.

louis-le-blanc-de-beaulieu.name: Louis Le Blanc de Beaulieu
louis-le-blanc-de-beaulieu.bio: Reformed professor of theology at the Academy of Sedan. His Theological Theses map Protestant and Roman Catholic positions with unusual clarity and restraint; John Owen praised his moderation on justification. Distinctive for irenic comparison without surrendering Reformed confession.

john-davenant.name: John Davenant
john-davenant.bio: Lady Margaret Professor at Cambridge, later Bishop of Salisbury, and a British delegate at the Synod of Dort. He defended Reformed predestination while arguing a broad sufficiency of Christ's death for all—an English moderate-orthodox line often linked with later hypothetical universalism.

robert-baron.name: Robert Baron
robert-baron.bio: Reformed philosophy professor at St Salvator's College, St Andrews. Philosophia theologiae ancillans treats philosophy as the handmaid of theology: scholastic metaphysics ordered to Reformed doctrinal ends, not free-standing speculation.

josue-de-la-place.name: Josué de la Place (Placeus)
josue-de-la-place.bio: Reformed professor at the Academy of Saumur. Best known for denying the immediate imputation of Adam's first sin, teaching mediate imputation instead—a signature Saumur position contested by stricter Reformed orthodoxy and later condemned in some synodical debates.

epiphanius-of-salamis.name: Epiphanius of Salamis
epiphanius-of-salamis.bio: Bishop of Salamis (Constantia) on Cyprus. Best known for the Panarion (Medicine Chest), a vast catalogue of heresies, with the Ancoratus as a shorter doctrinal anchor for the churches. A fierce defender of Nicene orthodoxy and monastic discipline.

nemesius-of-emesa.name: Nemesius of Emesa
nemesius-of-emesa.bio: Bishop of Emesa (Homs) writing near the end of the fourth century. On the Nature of Man joins Christian doctrine to Greek philosophical psychology—soul, body, providence, and free will—in a synthesis widely read in East and West.

julius-africanus.name: Julius Africanus
julius-africanus.bio: Sextus Julius Africanus, Christian chronographer and encyclopedist of the early third century. His Chronographiai ordered world history to the Incarnation; the Cesti (Embroidered Girdles) is a learned miscellany of military, medical, and technical lore of which only fragments survive.

serapion-of-antioch.name: Serapion of Antioch
serapion-of-antioch.bio: Bishop of Antioch around the turn of the third century. Surviving fragments show a churchman guarding apostolic teaching, including caution about which gospels the churches should read.

samuel-strimesius.name: Samuel Strimesius
samuel-strimesius.bio: Reformed doctor of theology and primary preacher in the church and university at Frankfurt an der Oder (Viadrina). He labored for ecclesiastical peace among Evangelicals, weighing Lutheran–Reformed controversies by Scripture, and wrote irenic Latin works including Ingenua in Controversias Evangelicorum (1708) and Ingenua in Arminianismum Inquisitio (1703). Distinctive as a Frankfurt (Oder) faculty voice that distinguishes fundamental consensus from less-than-fundamental dissent rather than recycling only the stricter Genevan or Puritan lines.

john-wesley.name: John Wesley
john-wesley.bio: Anglican priest and preacher. These sermons are a plain-English reading. Salvation by Faith keeps the 1872 text beside the reading. The later sermons keep the 1771 text beside the reading, so the argument and the scripture can be checked.

origen.name: Origen of Alexandria
origen.bio: Teacher at Alexandria and later Caesarea, and the first great Christian scholar of the Bible. He wrote commentaries, sermons and treatises on nearly every book of Scripture and compiled the Hexapla, a six-column Old Testament. He was tortured in the Decian persecution and died soon after.

irenaeus.name: Irenaeus of Lyons
irenaeus.bio: Bishop of Lyon in Gaul, who as a young man heard Polycarp of Smyrna. His Against Heresies answers the Gnostic teachers with the rule of faith and the succession of bishops. His theme of recapitulation sees Christ undoing Adam's fall by living through every stage of human life.

cyril-of-alexandria.name: Cyril of Alexandria
cyril-of-alexandria.bio: Bishop of Alexandria from 412. He led the case against Nestorius at the Council of Ephesus in 431, defending the title Mother of God and the single person of Christ, and wrote long commentaries on both Testaments.

julian-of-eclanum.name: Julian of Eclanum
julian-of-eclanum.bio: Bishop of Eclanum in southern Italy and the sharpest opponent of Augustine's late teaching on grace and original sin. Deposed for refusing to condemn Pelagius, he argued that human nature remains good and the will free. Much of his writing survives only inside Augustine's replies.

didymus-the-blind.name: Didymus the Blind
didymus-the-blind.bio: Blind from early childhood, he taught at Alexandria for decades; Jerome and Rufinus studied with him. He followed Origen in reading Scripture and was condemned with him in 553, so many of his works survive only in fragments.

justin-martyr.name: Justin Martyr
justin-martyr.bio: A philosopher from Samaria who became a Christian and taught in Rome. His two Apologies and his Dialogue with Trypho defend the faith to emperors and to a Jewish teacher. He was beheaded in Rome around 165.

tertullian.name: Tertullian
tertullian.bio: A writer of Carthage and the first major Christian author in Latin. He coined much of the Latin vocabulary of theology, including the word trinitas, and wrote sharply against Marcion, Praxeas and pagan Rome. Later in life he joined the strict New Prophecy movement.

clement-of-alexandria.name: Clement of Alexandria
clement-of-alexandria.bio: Teacher at Alexandria before Origen. His Exhortation, Instructor and Miscellanies present Christ as the true teacher and draw freely on Greek philosophy, which he saw as a preparation for the gospel.

ignatius-of-antioch.name: Ignatius of Antioch
ignatius-of-antioch.bio: Bishop of Antioch, taken to Rome under guard to die in the arena around 110. On the way he wrote seven letters to churches, urging unity around the bishop and insisting that Christ truly took flesh, suffered and rose.

clement-of-rome.name: Clement of Rome
clement-of-rome.bio: A leader of the church at Rome near the end of the first century. His letter to the Corinthians, written about 96, calls a divided church back to peace and order. It is among the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament.

cyprian.name: Cyprian of Carthage
cyprian.bio: Bishop of Carthage from about 248 and a martyr in 258. He led his church through the Decian persecution, wrote On the Unity of the Church, and argued over how to receive Christians who had lapsed under persecution.

lactantius.name: Lactantius
lactantius.bio: A teacher of Latin rhetoric who became tutor to Constantine's son Crispus. His Divine Institutes is the first attempt at a full Latin account of the Christian faith, written for educated pagans.

hermas.name: Hermas
hermas.bio: A Christian of Rome whose Shepherd records visions, commands and parables about repentance. It was widely read in the second century, and some churches treated it as Scripture.

athenagoras.name: Athenagoras
athenagoras.bio: An Athenian philosopher who addressed his Plea for the Christians to Marcus Aurelius and Commodus around 177, answering charges of atheism, cannibalism and incest. He also wrote On the Resurrection of the Dead.

theophilus-of-antioch.name: Theophilus of Antioch
theophilus-of-antioch.bio: Bishop of Antioch whose three books To Autolycus defend the faith to a pagan friend. He is the first known writer to call God, his Word and his Wisdom a triad.

novatian.name: Novatian
novatian.bio: A Roman presbyter and the first Roman theologian to write in Latin. His On the Trinity was careful and influential. After the Decian persecution he refused to readmit the lapsed and led a rival church.

hippolytus.name: Hippolytus
hippolytus.bio: A presbyter at Rome in the early third century who wrote in Greek. His Refutation of All Heresies traces heresies to Greek philosophy. He clashed with the bishops of Rome and died in exile in Sardinia.

arnobius.name: Arnobius
arnobius.bio: A teacher of rhetoric at Sicca in North Africa who became a Christian around 300 and wrote Against the Nations, a sharp attack on pagan religion. Lactantius was his student.

minucius-felix.name: Minucius Felix
minucius-felix.bio: A Roman lawyer whose Octavius is a dialogue in which a Christian answers a pagan friend's objections on a walk by the sea at Ostia.

polycarp-of-smyrna.name: Polycarp of Smyrna
polycarp-of-smyrna.bio: Bishop of Smyrna, said to have known the apostle John. His letter to the Philippians survives, and the account of his martyrdom around 155 is the oldest Christian martyr story outside the New Testament.

gregory-thaumaturgus.name: Gregory Thaumaturgus
gregory-thaumaturgus.bio: Gregory the Wonderworker, a student of Origen at Caesarea who became bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus. His farewell address to Origen gives a rare picture of how Origen taught.

methodius-of-olympus.name: Methodius of Olympus
methodius-of-olympus.bio: A bishop in Lycia who wrote the Banquet, a dialogue in praise of virginity modeled on Plato, and works on free will and the resurrection that answer Origen. Tradition says he died a martyr around 311.

cyril-of-jerusalem.name: Cyril of Jerusalem
cyril-of-jerusalem.bio: Bishop of Jerusalem in the later fourth century. His Catechetical Lectures, given to people preparing for baptism, explain the creed and the sacraments.

tatian.name: Tatian
tatian.bio: A Syrian student of Justin. His Address to the Greeks attacks Greek culture, and his Diatessaron wove the four Gospels into one account. He later led the strict Encratite movement.

melito-of-sardis.name: Melito of Sardis
melito-of-sardis.bio: Bishop of Sardis in Asia Minor. His Easter sermon On Pascha reads the Passover as a picture of Christ.

didache.name: The Didache
didache.bio: A short early Christian manual, probably from around 100, on the two ways of life and death, baptism, fasting, the Eucharist and church leaders.

barnabas.name: Barnabas
barnabas.bio: A letter from about 100, traditionally linked to Paul's companion Barnabas, that reads the Old Testament as pointing to Christ.

mathetes-epistle-to-diognetus.name: Letter to Diognetus
mathetes-epistle-to-diognetus.bio: An anonymous letter to an inquirer named Diognetus, probably from the second century, known for describing Christians as the soul of the world.

commodian.name: Commodian
commodian.bio: A Latin Christian poet, probably of the third century, whose verse Instructions and Poem on the Two Peoples call pagans and Christians to repentance.

evagrius-ponticus.name: Evagrius Ponticus
evagrius-ponticus.bio: A preacher at Constantinople who became a monk in the Egyptian desert. His short sayings on prayer and on the eight evil thoughts shaped Christian teaching on the spiritual life.

amphilochius-of-iconium.name: Amphilochius of Iconium
amphilochius-of-iconium.bio: Bishop of Iconium from 373, a cousin of Gregory of Nazianzus and a friend of Basil. He defended the full divinity of the Holy Spirit.

apollinaris-of-laodicea.name: Apollinaris of Laodicea
apollinaris-of-laodicea.bio: Bishop of Laodicea in Syria and a strong defender of Nicaea, whose teaching that Christ had no human mind was condemned in 381.

eustathius-of-antioch.name: Eustathius of Antioch
eustathius-of-antioch.bio: Bishop of Antioch at the Council of Nicaea in 325 and a firm opponent of Arius. He was deposed a few years later and died in exile.
